Introduction
Despite this work being theoretical, we use this introduction as a place to com-

ment on the connection to the experimental side of gravity. The first observation of
the gravitational-wave signal was GW150914 by a pair of detectors of the Laser In-
terferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO) in 2015 [1], and the new age of
astronomical observations began. The signal was produced by the merger of binary
black-hole system and as such it can not only carry the information about the parameters
of the black holes participating in the merger, but also about underlying theory itself, e.g.,
the propagation speed of the modes [2] or the second law of thermodynamics of black
holes [3]. So far, general relativity (GR) has described the gravitational signal of the
merger of black holes well [4]. However, with the next generations of gravitational-wave
detectors, the measurement precisions will increase, and remnants of the strong-field
regime are expected to surpass GR. These discrepancies will help us to understand the
gravitational theory on a more fundamental level. The aim of this thesis is to deepen
our understanding of theories extending GR. The thesis is organised as follows.

In Chapter 1, we elaborate a little on why there exists a pursuit for theories beyond
GR, but the means by which to do it is exactly through the gravitational waves. Many
techniques have been developed to do so. Particularly interesting is the study of the
quasinormal modes. These modes are present during the final stage, the ring down, of the
binary merger [5]. One of the ways how to obtain them is via the process of linearisation
of the field equations. Note that this is also how the gravitational waves were originally
predicted [6]. The common way towards the linear perturbations is within the metric
formulation [7]. However, this approach becomes vastly complicated for more involved
backgrounds. That is why another perspective on the geometry was employed. Instead of
using the metric tensor explicitly, it is convenient to introduce a null tetrad of vectors, in
which the metric is implicitly encoded. The so-called Newman–Penrose (NP) formalism
[8, 9] then rewrites the tensorial quantities as scalars, which presents a conceptual shift
in the description of geometry. The basics of this language are summarised in Chapter 2.
The NP formalism, as a useful mathematical tool, was used by Teukolsky to study the
linear perturbations on the Kerr background [10, 11], which represents a very realistic
and astrophysical setting. He managed to separate the differential equations governing
the perturbations and reduce the complexity of the problem to solving the second-order
ordinary differential equations for each mode.

The NP formalism also offers a geometric insight into the theory. In particular, the
Petrov classification [12], which is based on the classification of the Weyl curvature
tensor, is elegant in the language of the NP Weyl scalars. The main idea of the classifica-
tion is the construction of the tetrad to coincide with so-called principal null directions,
that is, the directions in which the Weyl tensor vanishes. More detailed interpretation is
discussed in Sec. 2.5. Another important NP scalars are the Ricci rotation coefficients,
which represent the change of the null tetrad in a point of spacetime. The most geomet-
rically transparent Ricci rotation coefficients are those describing the null congruences
generated by the null vectors of the tetrad. In particular, change in the null direction can
be interpreted as the deformation of the optical rays. Then the behaviour of the optical
rays can be described by their expansion, shear, and twist. In Chapter 3, we rewrite
important geometries in the NP formalism to build a geometric interpretation of the NP
scalars and use them as backgrounds for perturbations.

11



The aim of this thesis is to use the NP (or later Geroch–Held–Penrose (GHP))
formalism to formulate the linear perturbations in a modified theory of gravity, quadratic
gravity. The explicit perturbed field equation system with its derivation is presented in
Chapter 4. The field equations are written as the second order differential equations
for the Ricci curvature scalars as the unknown functions depending on the spacetime
coordinates. Such a formulation is useful for both theoretical point of view for studying
stability of quadratic gravity, but also for the experimental side of gravity since, for
example, the field equations in this form can be studied to obtain the quasinormal modes
of black holes.

In the last part, Chapter 5, we focus on specific exact solutions of quadratic gravity.
Exact solutions as such are in general a good benchmark to perturbation theory and
provide a controlled environment in which various ideas can be tested. Exact solutions
are very rare even in GR. Obtaining a new exact solution in quadratic gravity that is not
present in GR is significantly more difficult. Here, we present such a solution, which
is of spherical symmetry and couples with the cosmological constant. Moreover, we
examine spherical symmetry more generally with Frobenius analysis in a new coordinate
system and relate it to previous work [13, 14].

12



1 Modified theories of gravity
General relativity (GR), as a fundamental theory of gravity, has remained mostly

unchanged since its formulation [15] and is to this day the most accurate description of the
gravitational interaction. Together with the standard model of particle physics, it forms
a foundation of contemporary fundamental physics. It has been speculated for a long
time that GR cannot be a universal gravitational theory, and many modifications were
introduced early on [16, 17]. The main arguments are both theoretical and experimental.

The former usually includes extensive discussions of the existence of singularities
in the theory and their nature, renormalizability of the theory and UV completeness or
even interaction of the classical gravitational field with quantum fields [18]. Several
ideas were used to overcome these difficulties such as the framework of the quantum
field theory, higher-derivative theories, string theory, or loop quantum gravity.

On the experimental side, the accelerated expansion of the universe was a big surprise
that led to accepting the cosmological constant Λ to the theory as the source of dark
energy causing the accelerated expansion of the universe. However, its fundamental
nature remains unclear. There are also discrepancies on the level of galaxies and galaxy
clusters, and thus dark matter was introduced. On the other hand, there exist more
possibilities to go beyond GR than to introduce the dark universe.

To begin with, when talking about modifications, we need to present what action
is to be modified. The action that produces the Einstein field equations of GR is the
Einstein–Hilbert action,

1.1 Higher dimensional theories
The standard playground for GR is the (3 + 1)-dimensional manifold, where the

number 3 refers to the space-like dimensions, and the number 1 is the time-like dimension.
Naturally, one can play with this setup. For example, string theories are said to work in
10 (and more) dimensions. Then, the number of dimensions D can be kept arbitrary.
However, in order to describe the physical reality, the additional dimensions need to
be somehow hidden (compactified) on a wide range of scales. For example, taking
into account the Newtonian potential, the point-like source generates the potential with
the radial dependance r−(D−3), but stable planetary orbits require D = 4. Still, it is
interesting to look at other caveats of general dimension.

An interesting approach to higher-dimensional theories is the limit of large dimen-
sions to study a black-hole horizon and its potential quantum gravitational effects [20].
Due to the existence of black-hole solutions and the propagation of degrees of freedom
in D ≥ 4, one can investigate properties in the limit D →∞, where some calculations
are expected to be more manageable.

13



On the other hand, we can consider lower dimensions, e.g., 2+1 dimensional gravity.
It was shown that in this setup, gravity is perturbatively renormalizable [21] and the
action has the form of the Chern–Simons action, which is in fact a gauge theory and can
be obtained as an expansion of string theories [22]. For more information, see [23].

The key aspect of the 2 + 1 setting is that the curvature is fully determined by the
field equations since the Riemann and Ricci tensors possess the same number of degrees
of freedom. Thus, the dynamics is essentially different (or lacking) in that sense that the
vacuum solutions are strictly Minkowski or (anti-)de Sitter. More on the solutions in
2 + 1 gravity in [24].

1.2 Theories with additional fields
The natural way to extend GR is to introduce additional matter fields in the gravi-

tational sector. The simplest choice would be a scalar field commonly denoted φ, but
other choices such as vectors and rank-2 tensors are common too. An important part
(not only) of these theories is a screening mechanism, which suppresses the effects of
the novel fields on the well established GR scale, e.g., weak coupling.

1.2.3 Tensor-vector-scalar theories
The tensor-vector-scalar (TeVeS) theories contain both a scalar field φ and a vector

field Aa. A review of these types of theories can be found in [36]. This type of
theories is relevant because they introduce the covariant completion of MOND (Sec. 1.3).
Despite MOND’s success in explaining galactic rotation curves, it can hardly be applied
in cosmological settings, since it is a non-relativistic gravitational theory. Bekenstein,
extending the work of Sanders in the TeVeS, proposed a relativistic (TeVeS) theory with
a MOND limit for non-relativistic systems.

The gravitational part of the action in the TeVeS theory is split into gravitational
part Sg̃, vector part SA, and a scalar part Sφ, see [19],

S = Sg̃ + SA + Sφ , (1.5)

where g̃ is the so-called Bekenstein metric. The transformation to the physical metric g
is

gab = e−2φg̃ab − 2AaAb sinh 2φ . (1.6)

1.4 Higher-derivative theories
Higher-derivative theories, as a subclass of modified theories, are subject to ghosts

too. When talking about these ghosts in modified theories, we mean physical degrees of
freedom that come with modifications of gravity, this is in contrast to the case of the

energies unbounded from below. Let us elaborate on some important higher-derivative
theories, namely, f(R) theory [38] and the Stelle quadratic gravity [39, 40].

2 Newman–Penrose and GHP
formalisms

The Newman–Penrose (NP) formalism [9], as well as its GHP modification [48], are
based on projections of the tensorial (and non-tensorial) quantities onto the null frame
denoted as

(k, l,m, m̄) . (2.1)

The quantities in question are the Ricci tensor Rab and the Weyl tensor Cabcd, as well as
the derivatives of the tetrad itself. Vectors of the frame are often adapted for a symmetry
of the spacetime, and thus allow expressions to be simplified considerably. Additionally,
there is a conceptual shift to try to abandon non-physical coordinate-related degrees of
freedom and arrive at more invariant quantities.

In this chapter, we offer an outline of the NP and GHP formalisms from the construc-
tion of the null tetrad, introduction of the Ricci rotation coefficients and their connection
to the torsion, through the formulation of the curvature and related identities, and last
but not least, the differential operators that are commonly used.

2.1 Null tetrad and related quantities

Firstly, let us introduce what the null tetrad (k, l,m, m̄) actually is. The vectors k
and l are future-oriented null vectors, i.e.,

k · k = l · l = 0 , k · l = −1 , (2.2)

and m is a spacelike complex vector1 with the complex conjugation denoted as m̄.
Naturally, the spacelike vector m is perpendicular to the null directions

k ·m = l ·m = m ·m = 0 , (2.3)

and satisfies standard complex normalisation,

m · m̄ = 1 . (2.4)

In that case, any metric g of the four-dimensional Lorentzian manifold can be decom-
posed into these four directions (k, l,m, m̄) in the following way,

g = −kl− lk +mm̄+ m̄m . (2.5)

The graphical representation of the null tetrad is visualised in Fig. 2.1.

Obviously, the null tetrad is not unique, so there is a natural freedom in the choice

of the tetrad given by the Lorentz transformations. In particular, the transformations
that preserve the normalisation (2.5) are (see [49])

• null rotations with k fixed,

• spatial rotations in the transverse space,

• boost in the k-l plane,

2.5 Petrov classification

The null rotations (2.95) or (2.96) naturally transform the Weyl scalars resulting in
the fourth-order algebraic equation in complex variable parametrising such a rotation
in the case we want to obtain a specific value of Ψ4 or Ψ0, respectively. Taking the latter
(Eq. (2.96)), the transformation of the Weyl scalar Ψ0 is (see [49]),

Ψ0 → Ψ0 + 4EΨ1 + 6E2Ψ2 + 4E3Ψ3 + E4Ψ4 . (2.103)

The vector k is said to be a principal null direction (PND) if the corresponding Weyl
scalar Ψ0 vanishes,

Ψ0 = 0 . (2.104)

By the fundamental theorem of algebra, the transformation given by Eq. (2.103) has
exactly four roots including multiplicities, that is, the Weyl tensor has exactly four PNDs
including multiplicities. The Petrov type is determined by the coincidence pattern of
these roots.

Petrov type multiplicities description

I (1, 1, 1, 1) algebraically general
II (2, 1, 1) one repeated PND
III (3, 1) one triply repeated PND
D (2, 2) two repeated PNDs
N (4) one quadruply repeated PND
O conformally flat spacetime

The degeneration of the PND is well represented by the Penrose diagram depicted in
Fig. 2.2. Individual arrows represent the increase in the multiplicity of a particular PND.

30



Figure 2.2 The Penrose diagram of the degeneracy of the PND.

Since the Weyl scalars enter various expressions within this thesis, for example, as
backgrounds in the perturbations, we shall briefly discuss the physical interpretation of
the special Petrov types.

2.5.1 Type II – one repeated PND
There is one double-degenerate PND present. The gravitational field has a preferred

null direction with the enhanced symmetry. Radiation and Coulomb-like components
coexist, but the repeated PND behaves differently from the two simple ones. The
structure of the Weyl scalars using such a frame component is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = 0 , Ψ2,Ψ3,Ψ4 ̸= 0 . (2.105)

The typical example of GR exact spacetimes of this type is gravitational waves propa-
gating on type D backgrounds [52].

2.5.2 Type D – two repeated PNDs
The D stands for ‘degenerate’ since there are two doubly-repeated PNDs. It is very

common that the black holes are of this type, e.g., the Schwarzschild, Kerr, Reissner–
Nordström and other black-hole solutions [52]. The Goldberg–Sachs theorem [53, 54]
guarantees the PNDs are geodesic and shear-free. This leads directly to the separabil-
ity of the Hamilton–Jacobi, Klein–Gordon, Dirac, and Teukolsky equations on these
backgrounds. The structure of the Weyl scalars in such a case is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = Ψ3 = Ψ4 = 0 , Ψ2 ̸= 0 . (2.106)

2.5.3 Type III – one triply repeated PND
In contrast to the previous case, in this type there is a longitudinal gravitational field

present. The structure of the Weyl scalars is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = Ψ2 = 0 , Ψ3,Ψ4 ̸= 0 . (2.107)

The typical examples include gyratons. For more, see [52, 39].

31



2.5.4 Type N – quadruply repeated PND
Such a spacetime is commonly interpreted as a gravitational wave. There is only

one preferred null direction and that correspond to the direction of the null transversal
radiation in that spacetime. The structure of the Weyl scalars is

Ψ0 = Ψ1 = Ψ2 = Ψ3 = 0 , Ψ4 ̸= 0 . (2.108)

The typical GR type N spacetimes belong to the Kundt or Robinson–Trautman (RT)
class; see [52].

2.5.5 Type O – conformally flat spacetime
In the conformally flat spacetime, the Weyl tensor vanishes entirely. Such spacetimes

include de Sitter, anti-de Sitter, and Minkowski geometry i.e., maximally symmetric
spacetimes.

3 Non-twisting geometries
In the previous chapter, namely in Sec. 2.1.1, we introduced the Ricci rotation

coefficients. Usage of these coefficients is convenient, because they are directly related
to the physical interpretation of the investigated spacetime. Some of them inherently
describe the behaviour of the null tetrad and the associated null curves in the spacetime.
In particular, the null field is often interpreted as tangents of the optical rays — null
geodesics generated by the null vector field, e.g., k — whose possible deformations
are expansion Θ, twist A, and shear σ. Thus, these properties are encoded in the Ricci
rotation coefficients (2.11)–(2.18), see [49], namely geodesicity in the coefficients κ
(see Eq. (3.20) of Sec. 3.2),

κ = 0 , (3.1)
expansion Θ and twist A in the coefficient ρ,

ρ = − (Θ + iA) , (3.2)

and finally shear σ is directly denoted as the Ricci rotation coefficient σ (2.13). Naturally,
the condition for the non-twisting geometry is A = 0, which gives

ρ = ρ̄ , (3.3)

i.e., the Ricci rotation coefficient ρ is real. In the following section, we shall discuss
two important classes of geometries that satisfy such conditions, that is, spherically
symmetric settings and the near-horizon extremal Kerr metric, which is of the Kundt
type; see below.

The historically prominent classes of non-twisting geometries are the Kundt class
[56] and the Robinson–Trautman (RT) class [57, 58]. The Kundt class is more restrictive
in the sense that it sets all the optical scalars to zero, i.e.,

A = 0 , σ = 0 , ρ = 0 , (3.4)

while the RT class keeps the expansion Θ non-vanishing,

A = 0 , σ = 0 , ρ = −Θ . (3.5)

These geometric properties and related aspects are discussed below.

3.4 Spherical symmetry
Spherical symmetry represents an important and non-trivial constraint on the geom-

etry that is employed very often within investigating various theories of gravity. That
is because while the spherical symmetry is relatively restrictive, it still possesses rich
classes of solutions, especially in modified theories, as black holes, wormholes, naked
singularities, etc. Two natural questions that arise in the context of the modified theories
are whether the Schwarzschild solution is still the solution of the vacuum field equations
and whether this solution is still unique, i.e., the only spherically symmetric solution of
the vacuum field equations.

3.5 Kerr metric
The Kerr metric [65] describes the geometry of a stationary axially symmetric

rotating black hole with the mass M and the rotation parameter a. It solves the vacuum
Einstein equations with vanishing cosmological constant (Λ = 0), thus, the scalar
curvature R and the Ricci tensor Rab are identically zero, i.e., the Kerr spacetime is an
Einstein space, which means that the Bach tensor Bab is vanishing as well.

see (3.81) with (3.76), there exists also the non-twisting null geodesic congruence with
adapted frame [66, 67, 68]. Additionally, the near horizon geometry of Sec. 3.6 is of

4.3 Linear perturbations of Kerr black hole in quadratic
gravity (paper)

This section is in the form of the published paper [51], Š. Knoška, D. Kofroň, and R.
Švarc, Linear perturbations of Kerr black hole in quadratic gravity, Phys. Rev. D 112
104058 (2025). In this paper, the linearisation of the quadratic gravity field equations
is undertaken in the Kerr background, which is deemed highly astrophysically viable.
Such a background was taken notably by Teukolsky in GR [10, 11], where he considered
various matter contents, namely the electromagnetic or neutrino fields as sources for the
perturbations, or just effects of vacuum dynamical gravitational field. Interestingly, in
GR the equations for such fields decouple completely. In quadratic gravity, the motivation
is similar, our goal is to obtain the field equations for the dynamical gravitational field in
the Kerr background. In the following 11 pages, the Phys. Rev. D version of the paper
[51] is printed.

Employing the Newman-Penrose formalism and following the classic Teukolsky-like approach, we

linearize the field equations of quadratic gravity on the Kerr background and combine them with the

linearized Ricci and Bianchi identities. This leads to constraints on linear perturbations of the Kerr

spacetime in quadratic gravity. The resulting differential equations are decoupled in such a way that only

the Ricci tensor perturbations need to be found on the Kerr background in order to fully determine the

solution. The results are illustrated in the simple nontrivial cases of the Schwarzschild and Minkowski

geometries.

DOI: 10.1103/w3y1-ydq5

I. INTRODUCTION

The idea of modifying general relativity (GR) has been

reflected for a long time, beginning immediately after the

formulation of GR [1,2] and extending to the present day;

see, e.g., [3]. In general, we can conclude that modifica-

tions of GR are inevitable either from an observational

point of view [4,5] or from a purely theoretical perspective

[6,7]. The latter is concerned mainly with the ways of

extending GR in the strong-field regime. The natural way

of modifying GR is to introduce additional higher-curva-

ture terms to the Einstein-Hilbert action. This can be argued

as an effective field theory method. Namely, the quadratic

curvature terms, whose effects are investigated in this

paper, make the theory renormalizable [8] but the price

paid is to introduce so-called ghosts in the theory. These

ghosts propagate additional degrees of freedom, that is,

massive spin-0 and massive spin-2 mediators connected to

the presence of up to the fourth-order derivatives. Although

problematic, it is prospectively causal [9], and the physi-

cally relevant consequences can still be derived below the

cutoff energy scale.

The (Stelle) quadratic gravity [10] investigated in this

paper contains two prominent subclasses. One of them is

R2-theory that was of interest in the cosmological models

of inflation; see, e.g., [11]. The second one, Einstein-Weyl

gravity, extends the GR action by the square of the Weyl

tensor. Interestingly, it was shown that the gravitational

effects of the Weyl (spin-2) term can exceed those of the R2

(spin-0) in the case of compact stars [12].

The interesting and well-reasoned settings for studying

quadratic gravity implications are black holes. The astro-

physically most relevant case is represented by the Kerr

spacetime [13], which describes the geometry of a sta-

tionary axially symmetric rotating black hole. This setting

is shown to be the only GR stable rotating solution which is

astrophysically viable. Thus, there is much focus on finding

remnants of strong-field gravity extending GR in the Kerr

background, such as gravitational wave analysis [14] or

black-hole images [15]. Although available data are in

agreement with the Kerr properties, much is unknown with

respect to possible tiny discrepancies described by alter-

native theories. Here, Stelle’s quadratic gravity is a natural

candidate since the GR vacuum spacetimes themselves also

solve the field equations of quadratic gravity and thus

provide suitable backgrounds for perturbative analysis.

The perturbative approach is also closely related to the

study of spacetime stability, which is an important topic not

only in GR but also has been gaining interest within

modified gravity theories during the past years. For

example, starting with the Schwarzschild solution and

spherical perturbations, it was shown that small-mass black

holes (compared to theory constants) are unstable within

quadratic gravity [16]. A similar conclusion also holds for

the alternative branch of non-Schwarzschild spherically

symmetric black holes [17]. More recently, the nonradial

perturbations of spherically symmetric black holes were

studied in [18,19].

We aim to follow Teukolsky’s approach [20], where the

Newman-Penrose (NP) scalar quantities [21] are perturbed

rather than the metric coefficients. In general, this allows

one to perform a coordinate-independent analysis of the

perturbative modes. The NP formalism permits placing the

additional conditions on the perturbations, e.g., their

algebraic structure, existence and behavior of null geodesic

IV. SUMMARY

As our main result, we derive the differential equa-

tions (32) and (33)–(38) that constrain arbitrary perturba-

tions of the Kerr background governed by a generic

quadratic theory of gravity and can serve further in various

applications. All perturbations are encoded in terms of the

Ricci tensor projections. In general, we employ the

Newman-Penrose formalism, which provides the advantage

of coordinate-independent statements. Simultaneously, the

differential equations are of the second order, and thus their

analysis could become easier in comparison with the

fourth-order constraints in terms of the metric functions.

Moreover, the Ricci tensor projections, and subsequently

related Newman-Penrose scalars, can be connected to

physically relevant quantities, and specific viable assump-

tions can thus be directly performed with respect to a

particular situation to be described, e.g., algebraic structure,

behavior of test observers, spacetime symmetries, etc.

Finally, the Kerr background itself, as a vacuum solution

to general relativity, does not contribute to the Ricci

curvature, and thus its any nontrivial part immediately

arises as the quadratic gravity correction and can easily be

recognized.

As simple examples, the static radial perturbations of the

Minkowski and Schwarzschild geometries were presented

using this approach. However, a much more interesting and

technically challenging discussion of perturbations as, e.g.,

extension of complete Kerr spacetime within quadratic

gravity or effects of matter and dynamics even for simpler

backgrounds are postponed for further work. Also, a

similar stability analysis to that carried out in [18,19] will

be interesting starting with the Kerr background. Moreover,

in [33], an approximative slowly rotating black hole was

studied, concluding that two branches of solutions exist, the

classic Kerr branch and the additional quadratic-gravity

one. Investigating such a possibility within the presented

formalism could also give a deeper insight into the structure

of such solutions.

5 Exact solutions
Exact solutions of any theory of gravity occupy the privileged position in studying

the theory itself. Investigating such solutions reinforces the understanding of its fun-
damentals and improves the physical intuition in general. It is not surprising that the
exact solutions are as important in modified theories of gravity as in GR [49, 52]. Over
more than century, the well-known Schwarzschild solution [61] has demonstrated how
crucial an exact solution can be in the development of a theory. Here, the Schwarzschild
solution is mentioned also for the second reason and that is the underlying geometric
assumption, i.e., spherical symmetry. Although the axial symmetry of the Kerr solution
is more realistic, the increase in complexity of the solution is significant. Additionally,
higher-derivative theories bring new layers of challenges, so spherically symmetric ge-
ometries are prominently investigated as highly relevant spacetimes not only in quadratic
gravity.

5.1 Frobenius analysis of the exact solutions

allows more types of solutions [13, 45, 14, 46, 47]. The way these results were primarily

field equations can be expanded in a form of power series in a ‘radial’ variable of the

So far, in this chapter, only power series form of the solutions have been presented.

For specifically coupled values of the quadratic gravity parameters, we present a fully explicit static
spherically symmetric solution. It contains the central singularity surrounded by the black-hole or the
cosmological horizon for the negative or positive cosmological parameter, respectively. This spacetime,
thus, belongs to the already analyzed classes of solutions expressed in terms of the Frobenius expansions,
continuous fractions, or numerical simulations; however, it has not been explicitly identified before. The
purpose of the presented highly constrained somehow unphysical model is to reveal a global geometric
picture that may occur in spherical spacetimes within quadratic gravity, which is typically hidden in more
general approximative solutions. At the same time, it can serve as a solid benchmark for evaluating the
accuracy of the methods employed to obtain such solutions.

DOI: 10.1103/r9wy-ds11

I. INTRODUCTION

Modified theories of gravity have garnered considerable
attention over the past decade [1–4]. This follows from both
practical reasons for explaining observational phenomena
[5] and theoretical reasons for discovering mysteries of the
quantum theory of gravity. For the latter case, it is natural to
allow the quadratic terms in curvature to be present in the
action because these terms naturally arise from the semi-
classical limit of quantum stringlike theories. Additionally,
such action is renormalizable with the drawback of intro-
ducing ghosts into the theory [6].
The physically reasonable and natural setting to test the

consequences of quadratic gravity is to assume a static and
spherically symmetric spacetime. This allows us to study
generalizations of the classic Schwarzschild geometry [7].
Surprisingly, in contrast to the Birkhoff theorem in general
relativity (GR), many other (non-)black-hole solutions are
present in this setup [8–15] in addition to the Schwarzschild
one. Moreover, even with the restrictive spherical assu-
mption, the generalized non-Schwarzschild solutions with
the quadratic contribution present cannot be typically
expressed in terms of elementary functions, and various
techniques to obtain such solutions are employed, namely,
the Frobenius-like analysis of the power series, numerical
integration, or linearization of the equations in the weak-
field regime.

One of the most important questions discussed is the
asymptotic behavior of the black-hole solutions and
whether the asymptotically flat (black-hole) solution with
the Schwarzschild limit can even exist. This was inves-
tigated, e.g., in [8,9,16,17], and others. It was shown that
asymptotically flat black holes are very special. In fact, they
require some fine-tuning of the parameters.
As we have already mentioned, quadratic theory in the

spherically symmetric regime is richer than in GR and
allows for qualitatively different types of solutions. This
means that another important task is to identify and classify
all possible solutions. The detailed classification was carried
out using the conformal-to-Kundt coordinates [18] in [15].
These coordinates offer a surprisingly simple formulation of
the quadratic gravity field equations. However, the classi-
fication is not necessarily complete because it is based on
power series expansions, which are coordinate-dependent.
In particular, some coordinates do not allow the power series
expansion of a specific solution. Moreover, the Frobenius-
like solutions are limited by the convergence radii of the
series and can thus describe only the local behavior of the
geometry rather than its global structure.
Due to the complexity of quadratic gravity and the

richness of its solution space, even in the simple case of
spherical symmetry [19], its deeper understanding remains
an open problem. Therefore, the analysis of a fully explicit
global exact solution, which will be carried out in this
paper, seems very interesting, even though the price to pay
is a very specific coupling of the theory constants.
The paper is organized as follows: in the remaining part

of the Introduction, we summarize the description of
quadratic gravity and spherically symmetric geometries.

IV. CONCLUSION

In this work, we have identified and analyzed a fully
explicit static spherically symmetric solution in quadratic
gravity (1) under the assumption of constant scalar curva-
ture (5). Using the conformal-to-Kundt line element (13),
the metric functions that solve the field equations (7)
become (32) and (33) together with a special coupling
of the quadratic-gravity parameters (35) (see Sec. II). From
a geometric perspective, the solution contains a central
curvature singularity accompanied by either a black-hole
horizon or a cosmological horizon, depending on the sign
of the cosmological parameter Λ. Seen by the timelike

observer, the spacetime is thus split into two regions. These
aspects are illustrated by an explicit evaluation of the
curvature invariants and related analysis of the behavior of
geodesics.
Although this spacetime belongs to the previously

studied classes of spherical spacetimes in quadratic gravity,
typically described using (approximative) methods such as
infinite power series, continued fractions, or numerical
simulations, its explicit closed form had not been recog-
nized before. Here, we demonstrate its relation to
the extensively studied Frobenius expansions and show
the treacherousness hidden in the gauge choice and the
Schwarzschild-(anti-)de Sitter background identification
possibly restricting the convergence of the series.
Despite the highly constrained and physically limited

nature of the described model, it reveals a complete global
geometric structure and admits a very simple mathematical
form that is typically obscured in more general, however
typically approximate and enormously complicated, sol-
utions to quadratic gravity. As such, the solution may
provide a test bed for studies of more realistic situations
through a wide range of methods.

Conclusion
The main theme of this thesis is the study of selected geometries, both within the

perturbative Newman–Penrose (or Teukolsky-like) framework and through analytical
approach to specific exact solutions to quadratic gravity.

In Chapter 1, several prominent examples of modified theories of gravity are intro-
duced. Mainly the four types of modifications were mentioned, that is, dimensional
modifications, additional gravitational fields, modified Newtonian dynamics, and higher-
derivative theories, which receive the heaviest focus here, with special attention to
quadratic gravity. The variational principle is used to obtain the field equations and
important mathematical aspects of the theory are presented, for example, the modes
of propagation of degrees of freedom within the theory or that the Einstein spaces are
automatically solutions of the quadratic gravity field equations. The latter property
makes GR backgrounds natural candidates for backgrounds for perturbative treatment of
quadratic gravity theory. In this procedure small deviations caused by quadratic gravity
are expected to alter the standard GR geometry. In order to manage such calculations,
advanced mathematical tools are needed.

The primary language of the perturbations is the Newman–Penrose (or Geroch–
Held–Penrose) formalism. Therefore, we present the reformulation of geometry in
such language in Chapter 2. The advantage is that it provides a coordinate-independent
description and statements. All the necessary identities, relations, and definitions of the
Newman–Penrose formalism are presented there. Another important tool often used is
the Petrov classification of the Weyl tensor, which can further constrain the structure
of the backgrounds. Mainly, the type D of the Petrov classification is considered in
subsequent chapters. Therefore, the algebraic aspects of the curvature are summarised
here as well.

In Chapter 3, the notion of optical scalars is introduced. Then, in the context of the
NP scalars interpretation, the non-twisting geometries directly emerge from restrictive
conditions placed on these scalars. Naturally, selected classes of the non-twisting
geometries are fully presented in the Newman–Penrose formalism and used as the main
backgrounds for perturbations. From the non-twisting geometries, the parametrisation
of the Kerr background is excluded; however, the near-horizon geometry of an extremal
black hole is again manifestly non-twisting and thus is investigated within this chapter.

The main part of the original results of the thesis is presented in Chapter 4. We
use the Teukolsky-like approach to obtain the perturbative field equations in terms
of the Ricci tensor projections for various backgrounds. Starting with the simplest
choice of the (anti-)de Sitter background and continuing with the Schwarzschild and
Kerr backgrounds in the form of the published paper [51], we arrive at the general
Einstein space as the background for perturbations. With the derivatives introduced
within the Geroch–Held–Penrose formalism, the equations are in relatively compact
form. Additionally, they separate in the general Einstein space in terms of the projections
of the Ricci tensor, and with the Bianchi identities they form a complete set of differential
equations to solve. In other words, this set-up rewrites the fourth-order equations in the
metric to the second-order equations in the Ricci tensor projections.

In Chapter 5, the focus is on the exact solutions of quadratic gravity. Even the simplest
choice of the spherical symmetry is challenging to solve analytically, so the Frobenius
analysis is employed to discuss the admitted solution types in the various coordinate

103



systems. However, the Frobenius analysis covers only the radius of convergence of the
power series and thus this technique has limitations. Surprisingly, there exists a solution,
for which the power series is truncated, and such a solution of quadratic gravity with
non-vanishing cosmological constant is investigated in the second paper [74]. This fully
explicit solution can be used for further analysis in which the global properties play
significant role and the power series form of the solution is insufficient, e.g., geodesic
motion, compactifications, etc.

Finally, the main text is further guided by four technical appendices where supporting
calculations are performed.

The results of this thesis open several directions for future work. The most promising
and relevant is to use the perturbed field equations supplemented with other known
techniques to study the quasinormal mode behaviour governed by quadratic gravity. This
would directly confront quadratic gravity with astrophysical observational data from
future-generation gravitational wave detectors. The closely related topic is the question
of stability of the known solutions within quadratic gravity. If a vacuum GR solution
is stable with respect to Einstein’s field equations, the GR solution is not necessarily
stable in quadratic gravity. With the field equations presented in this work, stability
of the GR solutions against perturbation modes can be studied. Another direction of
future work is generating new approximate generalised counterpart solutions of general
relativity in quadratic gravity under physical assumptions about the desired geometry.
For example, the linearised version of the Schwarzschild–Bach solution as found as
the radial perturbation of the Schwarzschild background. We would like to explore
analogous extensions of the Kerr geometry.

C Conformal transformation
A conformal transformation is a transformation of the form

gab → g̃ab = Ω2(x)gab , (C.1)

where Ω is a positive function of the spacetime coordinates, and g̃ab is a conformally
related metric to the original metric gab. In general, a conformal transformation is not a
diffeomorphism, but some diffeomorphisms ψ can generate conformal isometry [75],

ψ∗gab = Ω2gab . (C.2)

abstracts.value: We give a general proof of the Rényi QNEC formulated using the Araki-Masuda weighted $L_p$ norms for all $p > 2$. This generalizes the algebraic proof of the QNEC applicable at $p=2$. Our approach utilizes a weighted version of a conditional $L_p$ norm which extrapolates the quantum expansion/ant-quantity. We elucidate some properties of the corresponding weighted conditional entropy both for half-sided modular inclusions and for general von Neumann subalgebras with a common cyclic and separating vector. The $p=2$ limit computes a conditional dynamical entropy originally defined in the context of black hole dynamics.

titles.title: Proof of the Rényi QNEC

abstracts.value: Variational second-order reduced-density-matrix calculations can dissociate molecules into fractionally charged fragments; Part I largely removed this failure with integer electron-count conditions on fixed partitions. Building on the realizability theory of point processes, we place these conditions in a convergent hierarchy of rigorous relaxations, defined by finite occupation linear programs (LPs) on spatial partitions, for real-space pair densities at fixed one-particle density. Every level contains all representable pair densities, the levels tighten under nested refinement, and their intersection characterizes pair densities admitting a symmetric $N$-particle probability-measure extension. In a fixed orbital basis the levels give monotonically increasing lower bounds to the full configuration-interaction energy, which they need not reach, even for the Coulomb repulsion. The spin-summed real-space cuts of Part I are its two-cell members. The LP optimum is also a measure: at fixed one-particle density it equals the $L^1$ distance of the coarse-grained candidate from representability and increases under refinement to that of the candidate, with a vanishing coarse-graining error; its primal law constructs a representable approximation, and its dual a violated valid inequality, used as a cut in molecular calculations. The count conditions are not implied by the usual positivity conditions: moment data that satisfy all three-particle positivity conditions, including $T_1$ and $T_2$, give through Gaussian orbitals a smooth pair density that violates an integer count. For atoms at fractional electron number, ensemble relaxations with the integer-count condition lie closer to the exact piecewise-linear energy than the zero-variance fixed-$N$ form.

titles.title: Integer electron-count cuts in variational second-order reduced-density-matrix theory. II. A convergent hierarchy of rigorous relaxations for real-space pair-density representability

We study the two-player hat game as a two-input, three-output non-local game. We calculate the quantum commuting value and show that it coincides with the quantum one. In particular, we show that 
\[ω_{\rm q}(H_2)=ω_{\mathrm{qc}}(H_2)=\frac{15+\sqrt{33}}{36}\approx 0.576238.\]
 We achieve the optimal quantum advantage using a shared non-maximally entangled qutrit state. To establish optimality, we exploit the game's symmetry under the dihedral group $D_8$ and apply its representation theory to substantially reduce the complexity of the underlying matrix problem. We also determine the no-signalling value $ω_{\mathrm{ns}}(H_2)=2/3$.

abstracts.value: We complete a proof of the quantum null energy condition (QNEC) in the mathematical framework of Half-Sided Translations and Modular Inclusions (HST/HSMI) removing an assumption that applied to previous proofs. Here we establish a theorem, which when translated to a physical setting implies that the relative entropy comparing the state of fields outside a stationary black hole with a Hartle-Hawking (HH) state is always a convex function of the horizon cut. Previous proofs only applied when a purification with finite null energy was available. We also obtain a QNEC generalization in which the HH Hilbert space is replaced with one based on a weight which is plausibly of relevance to evaporating black holes in flat space.

abstracts.value: We investigate the entanglement entropy of topological quantum states associated with $T_{d,\,dn}$ torus links in (2+1)-dimensional SU(2) Chern--Simons theory at level $k$. These links consist of $d$ components with pairwise linking number $n$, and the corresponding link-complement states provide a natural setting to study multipartite entanglement in topological quantum field theories. We analyze the semiclassical limit $k\to\infty$ of the entanglement entropy by deriving the asymptotic behavior of the moments of the reduced density matrix. To achieve this, we decompose the integrable-representation space into left-edge, right-edge, and bulk regions and employ the stationary-phase method to evaluate their respective contributions. We find that the leading asymptotic behavior is governed entirely by the two edge regions, while the bulk contribution is asymptotically suppressed. The resulting expression for the limiting entanglement entropy is given in terms of Hurwitz zeta functions and exhibits a dependence on the residue class of $k$ modulo $n$. We further investigate the dependence of the limiting entanglement entropy on the winding parameter $n$ and the number of link components $d$. In the large-$d$ limit, the entropy reduces to a binary entropy determined by two normalized weights associated with the left and right edges. Finally, we show that the two iterated limits, $k\to\infty$ and $d\to\infty$, commute, reproducing the result obtained previously by taking the large-party limit first.

titles.title: Semiclassical Asymptotics of Entanglement in Torus-Link States

abstracts.value: We construct quantum channels by averaging unitary shift conjugations with respect to $κ$-additive probability measures on measurable abelian groups. The channels act on the duals of operator algebras generated by shifts and bounded measurable multiplication operators. They preserve $κ$-additivity of quantum states and admit a weak-$*$ integral representation on this class. If the averaging measure vanishes on singletons, every output state is singular. In the appendix, we also establish the corresponding Fubini's theorem for $κ$-additive measures.

abstracts.value: We prove that a simple, self-contragredient, rational, $C_2$-cofinite, integer-graded holomorphic vertex operator superalgebra of CFT-type has zero odd part. We then prove that every nonvacuum simple current of a strongly rational VOA has strictly positive lowest conformal weight. This leads to a contradiction with Dong-Jiao-Xu's theorem on the positivity of categorical dimension.

abstracts.value: Which complex classical paths contribute to a real-time Feynman path integral? Picard-Lefschetz theory answers this question with the intersection numbers of the thimbles, which are notoriously hard to compute in infinite dimensions. We show that resurgence provides a practical alternative. We compute the asymptotic series of the real and complex classical paths to high order, with Feynman diagrams and with a transport recursion for the cumulants, and read off the adjacency of the classical paths from the divergent tails of the series with Borel-Padé methods. The South-East rule then turns adjacency into relevance. For a particle meeting a Rosen-Morse barrier, we identify the relevant complex classical paths in front of and behind the barrier, including the complex path that carries quantum tunnelling, follow ordinary and higher-order Stokes phenomena as the final point moves, and verify the predictions with the exact propagator. The resummed series reproduce the propagator with exponential accuracy. Finally, we outline how the expansion extends to relativistic path integrals governed by a Hamiltonian constraint.

titles.title: Real-Time Path Integral Resurgence: Which Classical Path Contributes?

abstracts.value: We describe the projective orbits of complex spinors from the point of view of the momentum map. We treat the irreducible spin modules in odd dimensions 1,3,5,7,9,11 and the half-spin modules in even dimensions 2,4,6,8,10,12,14, which are the only cases with finitely many orbits. In the Clifford--Fock model, we construct representatives as sums of pure basis spinors, and the coefficients are chosen so that the representative is a critical point of the squared norm of the momentum map. The resulting momentum values in a fixed Weyl chamber distinguish the orbits. Completeness follows from Vinberg's theory of graded Lie algebras and stabilizer actions, independently of the classical spinor classifications. We recover the classical counts of 1,1,1,2,3,5 orbits in the odd cases and 1,1,1,2,2,4,9 in the even cases, and compute the projective dimension of every orbit. In dimension fourteen we also determine the closure order of the orbits, using the fact that the minimum of the squared momentum norm increases strictly under degeneration.

titles.title: The finite projective classification of complex spinors via momentum maps

abstracts.value: Direct-product spacetimes offer a tractable route to exact solutions in gravity theories beyond general relativity. We study $n$-dimensional direct-product spacetimes of $(m_1+m_2)$, $(2+m)$, and $(2+\ldots+2)$ type in linear gravity, general pure quadratic-curvature gravity, and one of the recently proposed higher-dimensional extensions of conformal gravity, allowing the two-dimensional subspaces to have nonconstant curvature. We classify the resulting solution spaces and determine how the allowed geometries depend on the gravitational theory and, in quadratic gravity, on the curvature couplings. Metrics containing two-dimensional part(s) of nonconstant curvature are governed either by algebraic conditions on a curvature profile or, in one special class of quadratic gravity, by a differential equation. Relations governing metrics with only constant-curvature $m$-dimensional subspaces are purely algebraic. We further examine conformal relations to linear-gravity solutions, generalized Petrov types, and compatibility with electromagnetic sources. Particularly noteworthy is that standard static black-hole geometries are absent from the direct-product sector of the considered form of conformal gravity for $n>4$. Four- and six-dimensional cases are analyzed in detail, and explicit analytic solutions illustrating the resulting structure are presented whenever possible.

titles.title: Direct product geometries in $n$-dimensional linear, quadratic, and conformal gravity

abstracts.value: We introduce a class of two-dimensional tensor network states obtained by categorifying matrix product states. This procedure leads us to consider bond spaces provided by a 2-vector space associated with the 2-cells of the underlying lattice. Tensor network representations are then defined as module categories over the free monoidal category on a monoidal signature encoding the lattice geometry. We prove a fundamental theorem stating that two representations generating the same states with suitable open boundary conditions are equivalent as module categories. Finally, we introduce a notion of 2-injectivity, a categorified analogue of the injectivity condition for matrix product states.

titles.title: Higher tensor network states in two spatial dimensions: fundamental theorem for open boundary conditions

abstracts.value: We prove that every non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion category with property F is pseudo-unitary and weakly integral. In particular, every modular category with property F is weakly integral. Neither sphericality nor pseudo-unitarity is assumed. Passing to the Drinfeld centre extends the result to degenerate categories whose dimensions are positive on the intersection of the Müger centre with the adjoint subcategory; these include every braided fusion category with a pseudo-unitary Galois conjugate. Physically, the result connects the arithmetic of topological orders to the computational power of anyon braiding: non-integer squared total quantum dimension guarantees infinite braid group images, a necessary condition for universal quantum computation.

titles.title: Property F implies weak integrality for non-degenerate pivotal braided fusion categories

abstracts.value: Local anomaly polynomials describe local variations, but a normalized Green-Schwarz phase also depends on global background data. We explain this dependence for ten-dimensional three-sphere bundles of quaternionic lines over closed spin seven-manifolds. The backgrounds retain two specified $\mathrm{Spin}(16)$ gauge bundles and an integral differential trivialization on the base, including its boundary identifications. The trivialized class is the sum of half the first Pontryagin class of the tangent bundle and the second Chern class of the quaternionic line's underlying complex bundle. For these backgrounds, the calculation combines a generally nonzero local Green-Schwarz integral with a real eta invariant evaluated by a twelve-dimensional Atiyah-Patodi-Singer filling. Together, these terms determine an integral relative characteristic number; the additive response is one third of that number, modulo integers. When the base's third and fourth rational cohomology groups vanish, the response equals eight times the Crowley-Goette invariant, without assuming that the base is simply connected. A calibration using the actual quaternionic line bundle gives additive value one third on $\mathrm{Sp}(2)$, recovering the known third-root phase. Distinct integral String data on one fixed ten-manifold give all three phase values, showing which global background information the response can detect. The physical identifications retain their prescribed fermion data, while the separate application to integral topological modular forms and vertex operator superalgebras requires compatible integral lifts. The response calculation constructs neither a microscopic realization nor an equivalence of complete theories.

titles.title: Global Green-Schwarz response on quaternionic sphere bundles

abstracts.value: We study eigenstate fluctuations of the particle number in the nearest-neighbour free-fermion model on the periodic cubic lattice $(\mathbb{Z}/L\mathbb{Z})^d$. For every fixed dimension, every particle number, every subvolume, and every normalized energy eigenstate, we prove a bound of order $NL^{d-1}$ for the particle-number variance. The corresponding eigenstate-thermalization estimate is of order $L^{d-1}/(Nη^2)$ for fluctuations of relative size $η$. In particular, at positive particle density the bound decays as the inverse linear size. The proof decomposes the centered particle-number operator according to one-particle energy transfer and treats the zero- and nonzero-transfer components separately. The nonzero-transfer part is controlled by a sharp resonance bound, proved from Mann's theorem on relations among roots of unity, while the zero-transfer part is estimated by a Hilbert-Schmidt argument. These bounds are optimal in every dimension: the maximal nonzero-gap multiplicity has order $L^{d-1}$, and suitable many-body eigenstates realize matching variance lower bounds and show that the concentration bound cannot be improved in estimates uniform in the tolerance parameter.

titles.title: One-Particle Resonances and Eigenstate Thermalization in Periodic Free-Fermion Lattices

abstracts.value: We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and $\sqrt{\mathrm{iSWAP}}$ gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

abstracts.value: The BB84 monogamy-of-entanglement (MoE) game has numerous applications in quantum cryptography, including quantum key distribution, position verification, and unclonable encryption. In this short note, we improve the error threshold for parallel repetition with identical answer strings from the approximately $3.7\%$ certified by the original bound to the sharp threshold $(1-1/\sqrt2)/2\approx14.64\%$. When the players need not give identical answers, we also obtain exponential decay whenever the sum of their error tolerances is below this threshold. These bounds strengthen existing security reductions to the BB84 MoE game, improving security bounds and certified noise tolerances for cryptographic protocols.

titles.title: Sharp error tolerance of the monogamy-of-entanglement game

abstracts.value: The first highly significant detection of the polarization of the X-rays from the Black Hole X-ray Binary Cygnus X-1 revealed surprisingly strong polarization parallel to its radio jet. The observation is now commonly interpreted as resulting from the Comptonization of some lower frequency seed photons in a laterally extended corona. The emitting plasma is likely moving along the jet axis with a sizable fraction beta of the speed of light, amplifying the polarization degree. In this letter we address the question of how laterally extended the corona actually needs to be to account for the observations, and we calculate the required outflow velocities of velocity-stratified coronas as a function of the stationary-frame aspect ratio h=H/2R of cylindrical coronas of height H and radius R. We find that models with h lesser equal 0.8 and beta=0.5-0.9 at the top of the corona can give both the observed photon index of Gamma=1.6 and the observed 4% polarization parallel to the symmetry axis. We do not find suitable solutions for larger h. Given the constraints on h, we discuss the likely size of the corona, emphasizing that compact coronas close to the black hole are preferred as they can tap more efficiently into the gravitational energy and the rotational energy of the black hole, and are less exposed to their own emission reprocessed in the optically thick portion of the accretion flow.

titles.title: The shape and velocity of black hole coronas

abstracts.value: We investigate the effect of a quartic scalar self-interaction, $λ|ϕ|^4$, on a holographic superconductor in which non-linear electrodynamic couplings generate a superconducting dome containing an extended Lifshitz regime. The quartic interaction leaves the linearized scalar dynamics around the normal phase unchanged while modifying the non-linear solutions where the scalar field is large. As $λ$ increases, the solutions within the dome pass through three stages. The Lifshitz region shrinks until its scaling solution disappears at $λ^*$, leaving a no-AdS region, beyond whose edge the flows end before reaching any asymptotic region, and above $λ_c$ the dome consists entirely of asymptotically AdS hairy black holes. At the bottom of the dome we identify the point where the horizon value of the scalar field is largest, which we refer to as the critical point. There this value lies at the deepest symmetry-breaking minimum that the horizon effective potential, of Landau-Ginzburg form, can have. Unlike a conventional Landau-Ginzburg description, this interpretation rests on the scalar field at the horizon rather than on the boundary order parameter. Below $λ^*$, the constant scalar of the Lifshitz fixed point sits instead at the minimum of the effective potential of its asymptotic scaling region.

titles.title: Landau-Ginzburg Theory of a Holographic Superconductor: A Horizon Perspective on the Zero-Temperature Ground State

abstracts.value: Family selection in generator-model noise tomography, usually quoted as a property of the hardware, is a hypothesis test whose shot floor is closed form, $N^{*}=λ_{\mathrm{req}}/(r_{\mathrm{b}} S)^{2}$, controlled by the absolute bias $r_{\mathrm{b}} S$ rather than by the relative residual $r_{\mathrm{b}}$, and therefore computable for any device before a single shot is taken. The same computation prices the recovery gates, because the fingerprint that fixes a family's residual and the Fisher information that ranks the designs are read off the same map: there is no design-independent verdict and no family-independent design optimum. Whether a design can move that price is structural, not numerical: a bias confined to the block every design measures identically is design-blind, while one that reaches the code blocks can be repriced by a factor of sixty-eight. The two platforms here are its extremes, at $98.1\%$ and $48.0\%$ in the design-blind block. At the reference point the floor is $1.1\times10^{7}$ and $6.7\times10^{6}$ shots per component for the two families, so at the $10^{5}$ shots a run spends the test has power $0.053$ at a level of $0.05$ and the residual it reports is shot noise. Rebuilding the fingerprint under each of the sixty-four designs moves the floor by $68$ on one platform and $1.7$ on the other, and the most precise design costs ten times more shots for the verdict than the cheapest to test. All sixty-four placements are full rank, so the design problem is one of conditioning: at three gates the rms varies by factors of $2.7$ and $3.9$ with placement alone, while the optimum over counts is flat. At five qubits the same rule moves the floor by $21$, while the verdict itself costs $10^{9}$ shots; checked against the calibration of a real three-qubit register, the floor is a requirement on systematic control before it is a shot count.

titles.title: Model-family selection and recovery-gate design in generator-based noise tomography

abstracts.value: Extensions of $Λ$CDM that raise $H_0$ with additional energy before recombination, such as dark radiation and early dark energy (EDE), also raise $S_8$. We study whether a late-time energy exchange between the vacuum and the dark sector can offset this increase. The coupling rate scales as $\bar m H^α$ and is negligible before recombination for $α\le -2$; the energy is transferred along the four-velocity of geodesic cold dark matter, so the dark matter produced by the vacuum carries no density perturbation and slows the growth of structure. We add the exchange to dark radiation ($\bar m\tildeΛ$CDM) and to a one-parameter EDE model ($\bar m$EDE), and constrain the models with Planck 2018, DESI DR2 BAO and Pantheon+ data (CBS), and with the SH0ES calibration added (CBSH) to test the exchange when $H_0$ is held at a high value. For CBS the posteriors favour an energy flow from the vacuum into dark matter at 1.8-2.7$σ$, and the exchange lowers $S_8$ by 0.02-0.08 but does not raise $H_0$: $\bar m\tildeΛ$CDM gives $H_0 = 68.83 \pm 0.91$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, 3.1$σ$ below SH0ES. For CBSH the exchange removes the increase of $S_8$ caused by dark radiation, giving $S_8 = 0.800 \pm 0.016$ at $H_0 = 71.34 \pm 0.70$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, and about a third of that caused by EDE for $α= -2$, with the coupling at 1.1-2.0$σ$. The reduction of $S_8$ is concentrated at $z \lesssim 0.3$: at the redshifts probed by KiDS-Legacy the lensing amplitude decreases by only 1-2%, the shear $χ^2$ of the dark-radiation models changes by less than 3, and the exchange reduces but does not remove the excess shear $χ^2$ of EDE. A late-time exchange can therefore offset part of the $S_8$ increase of early-time solutions, but it does not ease the Hubble tension, and current data do not require it.

titles.title: Vacuum energy interacting with dark matter and dark radiation: alleviating the $H_0$-$S_8$ seesaw

abstracts.value: The tertiary invariant is a recently introduced pairing between two-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=(0,1)$ supersymmetric quantum field theories, motivated by topological modular forms. We evaluate it directly from its definition for the sigma models on $\mathrm{Sp}(2)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ with unit $H$-flux, paired with the internal theories of the non-supersymmetric $\mathfrak{so}(16)\oplus\mathfrak{so}(16)$ heterotic string and of the near-horizon region of the non-supersymmetric heterotic 6-brane, respectively. Regarding the target spaces as $S^3$ bundles over spheres, we fill in every fiber with a four-disk carrying a gauge instanton and reduce the invariant to the index of a Dirac operator on the base. We find nonzero values of order three and two, which determine the Green-Schwarz couplings of the two theories on $\mathrm{Sp}(2)$ and $\mathrm{SU}(3)$, respectively. The former, a $\mathbb{Z}_{3}$-valued discrete topological term of the $\mathfrak{so}(16)\oplus\mathfrak{so}(16)$ theory, was previously studied through anomaly inflow to NS5-branes. Our computation, which uses only the worldsheet theories, agrees exactly with that result and thus confirms the anomaly inflow.

abstracts.value: We extend the exact fixed-point tensor construction of Cheng et al. to fermionic minimal models, providing an analytic construction of fixed-point tensors for fermionic rational conformal field theories. The fermionic fixed-point tensor is defined as a correlation function of boundary-changing operators on a triangle, with careful treatment of fermionic parity and spin structure. Boundary tensors are also constructed and combined with triangle tensors to form strips, enabling the extraction of scaling dimensions for boundary-changing operators. The construction incorporates modified weights for shrinkable boundary conditions, systematic depiction of spin structures, recovering both the Neveu-Schwarz and Ramond sectors. As a benchmark, our tensor with a minimal truncation of descendant levels yields convergence to the exact bulk scaling dimensions of many low energy states for the free Majorana fermion ($c=1/2$), demonstrating the efficiency of approximate fixed point tensors from boundary changing operators. We also make use of a more general description of fermionic CFTs based on fermionisation of rational bosonic CFTs, and make a generic prescription for discretisation making use of their connections to modular tensor categories. We show that the discretised spin structures on a spin surface naturally recover the signs needed to recover the R/NS sectors. We propose that the collection of OPE coefficients of the discretised 2d CFT can be naturally interpreted as a state-sum of spin-TQFTs, analogous to the bosonic case. This work provides analytically computed starting points for tensor network simulations of fermionic critical phenomena.

titles.title: Discretising 2D Fermionic CFTs

abstracts.value: We investigate critical relaxation dynamics and their connection to quantum information scrambling in the conformal field theory dual to a Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter (RN-AdS) black hole. Employing the holographic dictionary, we formulate the thermodynamics in terms of boundary CFT variables and study the stochastic evolution of the reduced horizon radius using Langevin and Fokker-Planck formalisms. We demonstrate pronounced critical slowing down in the dual CFT, characterized by an enhancement of the autocorrelation time and stochastic fluctuations, accompanied by a suppression of the lowest nonzero Fokker-Planck eigenvalue. The autocorrelation time exhibits a universal power-law divergence, $τ\sim|ε|^{-Δ}$, with $Δ\simeq 2/3$, consistent with the analytical prediction and previous bulk gravitational results. Going beyond the conventional single-parameter analysis, we incorporate variations of the CFT central charge and identify a combined scaling variable involving temperature and central charge, demonstrating that the leading relaxation dynamics retain the same critical exponent along different trajectories in the two-dimensional parameter space. Finally, we explore the interplay between thermodynamic relaxation and quantum information scrambling by comparing the relaxation timescale with the fast-scrambling timescale. The comparison reveals a crossover between thermodynamic relaxation and quantum scrambling for which we derive the corresponding crossover scale analytically and find that, in the large-central-charge limit, it behaves as $\hatε\sim(C\ln C)^{-3/2}$. We also verify this numerically using the full nonlinear free-energy landscape. Our results connect critical dynamical scaling, finite-central-charge effects, and quantum scrambling within the holographic CFT framework.

titles.title: Critical Slowing Down and the Crossover to Quantum Scrambling in Holographic CFTs

abstracts.value: The microscopic origin of the deuteron tensor polarized structure function $b_1$ remains unresolved. Conventional nuclear models attribute a nonzero $b_1$ mainly to the $D$-wave component of the deuteron wave function, but generally fail to reproduce the magnitude and momentum-dependence observed by the HERMES experiment. Using a QCD-based light-front framework with degrees of freedom beyond the conventional nucleonic picture, in particular including hidden-color components and relativistic spin--momentum correlations, we find that a small but nonzero estimated hidden-color admixture can be sufficient to generate a substantial tensor response ($b_1(x)$), while it is essentially insensitive to the $D$-wave component. The physical $D$-wave probability of $0.85\%$, fixed by the empirical quadrupole moment, changes $b_1$ by only $1.7\%$, with the dominant contribution arising from the colored-cluster $S$-wave sector. These results demonstrate that the tensor-polarized structure of the deuteron is driven primarily by hidden-color dynamics rather than by the $D$-wave component.

titles.title: Origin of Tensor Polarized Structure of the Deuteron

abstracts.value: A regular black-hole metric need not define a regular configuration of VCDM, whose preferred foliation is part of the gravitational solution. We construct stationary rotating, possibly charged configurations on the constant-auxiliary Einstein-Maxwell branch. Their Kerr-Newman and Kerr-Newman-de Sitter geometries carry nonzero constant-mean-curvature foliations that cross the future black-hole horizon and, in the de Sitter case, the future cosmological horizon. A horizon-regular flux formulation specifies the inner data and the distinct hyperboloidal and expanding asymptotic ends. Seventeen survey configurations are supplemented by a mean-flux scan at fixed four-geometry and paired flat/de Sitter comparisons down to $κM = 0.01$, where $K_0 = 3κ$. Varying the flux changes the preferred-foliation shear without changing the background seen by standard test matter. The paired local lapse and shear differences have effective powers close to two over the computed range, with the lapse comparison requiring a fixed time normalization. Continuous residuals, geometric reconstructions, and selected grid comparisons test the numerical solutions. An exact lapse bound excludes zeros in the regular stationary exterior block with $Δ_r > 0$. We distinguish singular finite-proper-distance endpoints from asymptotic trumpet ends and give conditional bounds on a stationary spacelike inner limit. A local cosmological interpretation requires additional matching assumptions; dynamical selection and the rotating interior endpoint are not determined by the stationary construction.

titles.title: Horizon-penetrating rotating black-hole configurations in VCDM

abstracts.value: We investigate the gravitational interaction between primordial radiation, consisting of photons and ultra-relativistic neutrinos, and primordial black holes (PBHs), and study its imprint on the anisotropies of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Assuming that PBHs are immersed in the cosmic radiation background, we introduce a covariant energy-momentum transfer four-vector to describe the gravitational capture of radiation by PBHs. We extend the background-level framework of M. Farhang and S. M. S. Movahed [Phys. Rev. D 114, 083533 (2026)] to an inhomogeneous Universe at linear order by consistently modifying the perturbed continuity and Euler equations to account for both energy and momentum transfer. We use the imprint of this interaction on the CMB to place novel constraints on the PBH abundance, $f_{\rm pbh}$. We show that these constraints are up to two orders of magnitude tighter than those obtained from background-only analyses and exhibit a strong dependence on the PBH mass. Using Planck temperature and polarization data, we constrain the PBH fraction to $f_{\rm pbh} \lesssim 0.05-0.002$ for $M$ in the range $10^{15}-10^{17} M_\odot$. Furthermore, sensitivity forecasts for a cosmic-variance-limited survey with $\ell_{\rm max}=7000$, assuming a fiducial $f_{\rm pbh}=0$, yield projected bounds of $f_{\rm pbh} \lesssim 10^{-2}-2\times 10^{-4}$ over the mass range $10^{13}-10^{17} M_\odot$.

abstracts.value: In this paper, we introduce the Angular Rotational Counter (ARC), a novel approach to represent objective functions that can be decomposed as a weighted sum of Boolean functions. ARC encodes the objective as an accumulated sum of quantum rotations onto a single-qubit register instead of a multi-qubit register used in much of the previous literature. We mathematically establish and experimentally validate that these rotations sum to the objective value for all possible solutions and derive the relationship between the resulting measurement probabilities and the objective. This design was applied to construct a quantum oracle for the state assignment problem of finite automata and state machines using a weighted Hamming distance cost function, which is a special case of the quadratic assignment problem. We evaluate this oracle design on 26 benchmarks and compare it with corresponding Boolean-based oracles on four cost metrics. Across these benchmarks, the oracle with ARC produces a mean reduction in the qubit count of 20.8%, gate count of 89.3%, circuit depth of 92.4%, and quantum cost of 90.6%. These results demonstrate substantial reductions in circuit cost for the evaluated benchmarks and establish rotational encoding as a promising approach for representing objective functions in optimization based on quantum search algorithms.

titles.title: Rotational Encoding of Objective Functions for Quantum Optimization

abstracts.value: Extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs) pose a major challenge to Bayesian parameter inference because of their complex, highly multimodal likelihood surfaces. Locating narrow high-likelihood regions is particularly difficult without knowledge of the true source parameters, which is unavailable in real observations. We develop a deep-learning-assisted Bayesian inference framework that combines neural-network-guided parameter-space localization, particle swarm optimization, and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Applied to simulated six-month EMRI signals, the framework recovers posterior distributions in close agreement with reference MCMC analyses initialized near the true parameter values, without requiring such knowledge for initialization. Once the neural network has been trained, the complete inference pipeline takes approximately 10 hours per signal.

titles.title: Deep-Learning-Assisted Bayesian Inference for Extreme-Mass-Ratio Inspirals

abstracts.value: The Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) code possesses a lattice periodic structure that enables the effective correction of small displacement errors induced by noise in phase space, which is indispensable for quantum computation. The GKP code was also used to construct a long-distance entanglement channel in quantum repeaters and distribute random keys in quantum key distribution (QKD). Using GKP encoding, we propose a quantum secure direct communication (QSDC) protocol that not only transmits the secret message directly, but also helps protect the safety of communication personnel. The exponential attenuation loss of photons can be overcome by the third-generation quantum repeater. Numerical simulation results demonstrate that secure transmission distance exceeding 1000 km is achievable with a 23 dB squeezing level. Furthermore, we establish a cost-based optimization framework to characterize the trade-off among secure communication distance, secrecy capacity, and repeater resources, enabling optimized repeater deployment and providing a systematic design strategy for scalable quantum repeater architectures. The results demonstrate the potential of combining GKP error correction for long-distance QSDC and quantum networks.

titles.title: Long-distance quantum secure direct communication with Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubits

abstracts.value: We investigate the stability of homogeneous chiral condensates in magnetized quark matter within the two-flavor Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model. By expanding the effective action to quadratic order, we derive the full momentum-dependent bosonic two-point function in a constant magnetic field. At zero temperature, our analytical results show that each occupied Landau level produces a sharp logarithmic divergence at its corresponding Fermi momentum. This severe Peierls instability is driven by one-dimensional Fermi surface nesting within the effectively 1+1-dimensional subsystems created by Landau quantization. Numerically, we map out the momentum-space topography of the two-point function across varying magnetic fields and temperatures. We find that strong magnetic fields induce deep negative canyons. While thermal fluctuations smooth these canyons into shallower valleys as the temperature increases, the negative regions remain robust at intermediate temperatures and only vanish entirely at sufficiently high temperatures. Intriguingly, at larger chemical potentials where the system is strictly stable, a broad positive basin with a flat curvature at the origin persists at non-zero momentum. This non-monotonic dispersion is the hallmark of a moat regime, acting as a precursor state that strongly signals a residual tendency toward inhomogeneous chiral symmetry breaking. Our findings provide valuable insights into the phase structure of dense, magnetized quark matter.

titles.title: Probing the inhomogeneous phases in magnetized quark matter via the bosonic two-point function

abstracts.value: The spin correlation of $Λ\barΛ$ hyperon pairs produced in heavy-ion collisions is investigated through scalar and pseudo-scalar mesonic channels that mediate the creation of $s\bar{s}$ pairs. Because a $J=0$ meson forces $L=S$ while parity requires $(-1)^{L+1}=+/-1$, the two vertices project the pair onto distinct total-spin states: a scalar ($0^+$) vertex selects the $L=S=1$ configuration with a spin weight of $+1$, whereas a pseudo-scalar ($0^-$) vertex selects the $L=S=0$ configuration with a weight of $-3$; these weights are the traces of the correlation tensor, corresponding to $P_{s\bar{s}}=+1/3$ and $-1$, respectively. Implementing this framework within the three-flavor Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model at the Random-Phase-Approximation level, we compute the scalar and pseudo-scalar spectral weights. Our results show that the pseudo-scalar channel dominates, resulting in a negative net correlation fraction throughout. And the spin correlation also depends on the opening angle: strongest spin correlation at around $θ=0$ while weakest at $θ=π$. Furthermore, we show that the collision-energy dependence of the momentum-integrated spin correlation along the freeze-out line is sensitive to the trajectory's path relative to the chiral phase boundary. Trajectories passing near the crossover region exhibit a non-monotonic structure, providing a sensitive probe for the location of the chiral phase transition.

titles.title: Interplay of Scalar and Pseudo-Scalar Mesonic Channels in $Λ\barΛ$ Spin Correlations
